questions.stem: The graphs of \(y=ax\) and \(y=\tan^{-1}(bx)\) intersect at three distinct points if:
questions.hint: Compare the gradient of tan⁻¹(bx) at the origin (= b) with the gradient of the line (= a).

steps.explain: Both graphs pass through the origin, and both are odd functions, so other intersections come in a pair \(\pm x_0\).
Gradient of \(y=\tan^{-1}(bx)\) at the origin:

\(\tan^{-1}(bx)\) flattens out towards \(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\), while the line keeps going. So there are two extra crossings only if the curve leaves the origin more steeply than the line, in the same direction: \(b\) and \(a\) have the same sign and \(|b|\gt|a|\).
Of the options only \(b\lt a\lt 0\) fits (option A, \(0\lt b\lt a\), has the line steeper — only one intersection).

meta.source: Baulkham Hills 2020 3U Trials & Solutions

keyPoints.note: The inverse-tan curve must start steeper than the line (|b| > |a|, same sign) so it can cross back.

questions.stem: The graph of the function \(y=\cos^{-1}(2x)\) is dilated horizontally by a dilation factor of 4 and then translated vertically by 3 units. What is its new equation?
questions.hint: Horizontal dilation factor k: x → x/k. Vertical translation: add outside the function.

steps.explain: A horizontal dilation by factor 4 replaces \(x\) by \(\frac{x}{4}\).
A vertical translation by 3 adds 3 to the whole function.
Multiplying \(x\) by 4 (option C) would compress the graph, not stretch it; adding 3 inside the brackets is a horizontal shift.

parts.stem: Sketch the graph of the function \(y=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-2}{2}\right)\), showing clearly the intercepts on the axes and the equations of the asymptotes.
parts.hint: Find the intercepts by setting \(x=0\) and \(y=0\); the horizontal asymptotes remain \(y=\pm\frac\pi2\).

steps.explain: Start with the parent curve \(y=\tan^{-1}u\): it is increasing, passes through \((0,0)\), and has horizontal asymptotes \(y=\pm\frac\pi2\). Here \(u=\frac12(x-2)\).
The horizontal shift and scale move the zero of the input to \(x=2\); the vertical asymptotes remain unchanged.
Find the y-intercept by setting \(x=0\). Mark both intercepts and the asymptotes, then draw a smooth increasing arctangent curve through them.

parts.stem: The graph of the function \(y=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-2}{2}\right)\) is transformed by a translation left by 1 unit, then a horizontal dilation with a scale factor 2. Find the equation of the transformed graph.
parts.hint: For a left translation by 1, substitute \(x+1\); for a horizontal dilation by 2, then substitute \(x/2\). Keep the whole input to \(\tan^{-1}\) grouped.

steps.explain: Translating the graph left by 1 replaces the input \(x\) by \(x+1\).
A horizontal dilation by scale factor 2 replaces the input in the translated equation by \(\frac{x}{2}\).
Simplify the argument before identifying the transformed equation.
This is option D. The order matters because the translation is applied before the dilation.

questions.stem: Consider the graph of \(y=f(x)\) shown here. Which one of the following would have 2 more roots than \(f(x)\)?
questions.hint: The graph has ONE root (x-intercept). Which transformation changes the number of x-intercepts? Look at the turning points: the local maximum is at about \(y=-2\).

steps.explain: The graph of \(f\) crosses the x-axis once (at \(x=2\)). Its local maximum is below the axis (\(y\approx-2\)) and its local minimum is also below the axis.
Shift up by 3: \(f(x)+3\) raises the local maximum above the axis (\(-2+3=1>0\)) while the local minimum (\(\approx-3.2+3<0\)) stays just below it. The curve now crosses the axis THREE times.

The others keep ONE root: \(-2f(x)\) (vertical stretch/reflection keeps the roots), \(f(x+3)\) (horizontal shift keeps the number of roots) and \(f^{-1}(x)\) (reflection in \(y=x\): the x-intercepts of \(f^{-1}\) are the y-intercepts of \(f\), only one).
So \(y=f(x)+3\) → B

keyPoints.note: Compare the turning points with the x-axis after each transformation.

questions.stem: Consider the function \(f(x)=2\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\). Evaluate \(f(3)\).
questions.hint: Substitute \(x=3\) so the bracket becomes \(\dfrac{3}{3}=1\). Then find the angle between \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) whose sine is 1.

steps.explain: Replace \(x\) by 3.
Simplify the fraction inside the bracket: \(\dfrac{3}{3}=1\).
\(\sin^{-1}(1)\) is the angle in \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) whose sine is 1. That angle is \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (\(90^{\circ}\)).
Multiply by 2.
So \(f(3)=\pi\), the top right end point of the graph. Option B forgets the factor 2.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Inverse sine returns an angle: sin inverse of 1 is pi over 2.

questions.stem: Consider the function \(f(x)=2\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\). Sketch the graph of \(y=f(x)\), showing the intercept and the coordinates of the end points. Which diagram (A, B, C or D in the figure) is correct?
questions.hint: Find the domain from \(-1\le\dfrac{x}{3}\le 1\), then evaluate \(f\) at the two end values of \(x\) and at \(x=0\).

steps.explain: The inverse sine is only defined for inputs from \(-1\) to \(1\). So \(-1\le\dfrac{x}{3}\le 1\); multiply by 3 to get the domain.
End points: \(f(3)=2\sin^{-1}(1)=2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\pi\) and \(f(-3)=2\sin^{-1}(-1)=2\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=-\pi\).
Intercept: at \(x=0\), \(f(0)=2\sin^{-1}(0)=0\). The graph passes through the origin, which is both the \(x\)- and \(y\)-intercept.
Shape: inverse sine is increasing, so the graph rises from the lower-left end point through the origin to the upper-right end point, steepest at the ends.

Compare: B has end points \((\pm 3,\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2})\) (missing the factor 2); C is \(2\cos^{-1}\) (decreasing, not through the origin); D has domain \([-1,1]\) (the \(\dfrac{x}{3}\) was ignored). Only A matches.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Domain from the bracket between minus 1 and 1; end points and the origin fix the sketch.

questions.stem: Consider the function \(f(x)=2\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\). State the domain and range of \(y=f(x)\) using the interval notation.
questions.hint: DOMAIN = allowed \(x\)-values (inside the bracket must be in \([-1,1]\)). RANGE = \(y\)-values the graph reaches (from the end points).

steps.explain: Domain: \(\sin^{-1}\) accepts only inputs from \(-1\) to \(1\), so \(\dfrac{x}{3}\) must be in that interval. Multiply by 3.
In interval notation (square brackets because the end points \(\pm 3\) are included).
Range: the output of \(\sin^{-1}\) is always in \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\). Multiply by 2 for \(f\).
In interval notation, and check against the end points \((\pm 3,\pm\pi)\) on the graph (green band on the \(x\)-axis, orange band on the \(y\)-axis).
Option C forgets the factor 2 on the range; option B uses the domain of \(\sin^{-1}x\) (not \(\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3}\)); option D swaps domain and range.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: The graph of an inverse trigonometric function is shown. What is the equation of this function?
questions.hint: \(y=\cos^{-1}(\text{something})\) needs the something to lie between \(-1\) and \(1\). The graph shows the domain is \(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}\); find the scaling of \(x\) that squeezes this into \([-1,1]\).

steps.explain: Read the graph: it passes through \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4},\pi\right)\), \(\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},0\right)\) (red points); the \(y\)-values run from \(\pi\) down to 0, exactly the range of \(\cos^{-1}\).

The range \([0,\pi]\) is unchanged, so the transformation is horizontal: \(x\) is scaled. We need \(-1\le\text{(inside)}\le1\) when \(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Multiply by 4 then divide by \(\pi\).

So the function is \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4x}{\pi}\right)\). Check: \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\Rightarrow\cos^{-1}(1)=0\) ✓; \(x=0\Rightarrow\cos^{-1}0=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) ✓; \(x=-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\Rightarrow\cos^{-1}(-1)=\pi\) ✓.
Why not the others: A and B multiply the OUTPUT (the range would no longer be \([0,\pi]\)); D has the inside \(\dfrac{\pi x}{4}\), giving domain \(\left[-\dfrac{4}{\pi},\dfrac{4}{\pi}\right]\).
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: Squeeze the domain into minus one to one inside the inverse cosine.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the graph of \(y=\sin^{-1}(\sin x)\)?
questions.hint: \(\sin^{-1}\) always gives an answer between \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). The inner \(\sin x\) is periodic, so the answer is NOT just \(x\) except when \(x\) is in that range. Test a few values: \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\).

steps.explain: Range: \(\sin^{-1}u\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), so \(y\) never leaves this band. This rules out the straight line \(y=x\) (graph B), which continues forever.

For \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(\sin^{-1}(\sin x)=x\) (the identity), so the graph is the line \(y=x\) from \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) to \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

For \(x=\pi\): \(\sin\pi=0\), so \(y=\sin^{-1}0=0\). For \(x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\): \(\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}=-1\), so \(y=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). The graph turns back down: a TRIANGLE (zig-zag) wave of period \(2\pi\) and amplitude \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

Compare the graphs: A is just the segment of \(y=x\) on \([-1,1]\) (this is \(\sin(\sin^{-1}x)\), the other order); B is the whole line \(y=x\); D is a wave between 0 and \(\pi\) (the graph of \(\cos^{-1}(\cos x)\)). Only C is the zig-zag between \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
So the correct choice is option C.

questions.stem: Sketch the graph of the function \(f(x)=-2\tan^{-1}x\) showing the intercepts on the axes and the equations of the asymptotes. Which sketch is correct?
questions.hint: Start with \(y=\tan^{-1}x\): increasing, through the origin, horizontal asymptotes \(y=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Then apply \(-2\times\): a reflection in the \(x\)-axis (decreasing) and a vertical stretch by 2 (asymptotes double).

steps.explain: \(y=\tan^{-1}x\): passes through \((0,0)\), is increasing, with horizontal asymptotes \(y=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (right) and \(y=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (left).
Multiply by 2: vertical stretch, so the asymptotes become \(y=\pm\pi\). Multiply by \(-1\): reflect in the \(x\)-axis, so the graph now DEcreases.
Intercepts: \(f(0)=-2\tan^{-1}0=0\): the graph passes through the origin (the only intercept, both the \(x\)- and \(y\)-intercept).
Why not the others: B is \(+2\tan^{-1}x\) (increasing); C has asymptotes \(\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (\(-\tan^{-1}x\)); D has asymptotes \(\pm\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) (a compression by \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Consider the function \(y=\cos^{-1}(\sin x)\). State the domain and range for this function.
questions.hint: \(\cos^{-1}(\ldots)\) needs an input between \(-1\) and \(1\) and gives an output between \(0\) and \(\pi\). The input here is \(\sin x\). Is \(\sin x\) always between \(-1\) and \(1\)?

steps.explain: Domain: \(\cos^{-1}(\sin x)\) needs \(-1\le\sin x\le1\). This is TRUE for every real \(x\), so there is no restriction.
Range: \(\sin x\) takes every value from \(-1\) to \(1\). \(\cos^{-1}(-1)=\pi\) and \(\cos^{-1}(1)=0\); \(\cos^{-1}\) is decreasing, so outputs fill \(0\) to \(\pi\).
So the range is \(0\le y\le\pi\).
Why not the others: B confuses the domain of \(\cos^{-1}\) (\(-1\le\) input \(\le1\)) with the domain in \(x\); C is the range of \(\sin^{-1}\); D mixes domain and range.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Consider the function \(y=\cos^{-1}(\sin x)\). Sketch the function over the domain \(0\le x\le2\pi\). Which sketch is correct?
questions.hint: Plot key points: use \(x=0,\dfrac{\pi}{2},\pi,\dfrac{3\pi}{2},2\pi\) where \(\sin x=0,1,0,-1,0\), and then \(\cos^{-1}\): \(\cos^{-1}0=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(\cos^{-1}1=0\), \(\cos^{-1}(-1)=\pi\). The gradient is always \(\pm1\), so join the points with STRAIGHT lines.

steps.explain: Calculate \(\sin x\) at the key \(x\)-values, then take \(\cos^{-1}\).
From part (i): the gradient is \(-1\) where \(\cos x>0\) (for \(0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}<x<2\pi\)) and \(+1\) where \(\cos x<0\) (for \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}<x<\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\)).

Plot the five points and join with straight lines: down from \(\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) to \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)\), UP to \(\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\pi\right)\), down to \(\left(2\pi,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\): a zig-zag (triangle wave) with sharp corners.
Why not the others: B is a smooth sine curve (the gradient is not constant); C is \(\cos^{-1}(\cos x)\) (starts at 0, not \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)); D is the vertical flip \(\pi-y\).
So the correct choice is option A.

Range: \(0\le\cos^{-1}(\ldots)\le\pi\). The factor 2 stretches vertically.
Compare: A has domain \([0,4]\), range \([0,2\pi]\), decreasing ✓. B has domain \([0,1]\) (wrong); C and D are INCREASING (they are graphs of \(2\sin^{-1}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Which graph shows the curve \(y=\sin^{-1}(x+1)\)?
questions.hint: Start from \(y=\sin^{-1}x\) (domain \([-1,1]\), range \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\)). Replacing \(x\) by \(x+1\) is a shift ONE UNIT LEFT. Only the \(x\)-values change; the range stays the same.

steps.explain: The basic curve \(y=\sin^{-1}x\) (grey dashed) runs from \((-1,-\dfrac{\pi}{2})\) through \((0,0)\) to \((1,\dfrac{\pi}{2})\).
\(y=\sin^{-1}(x+1)\): the input is \(x+1\), which must lie in \([-1,1]\). Solve this inequality for \(x\).
The range is NOT affected by a horizontal shift: \(y\) still goes from \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) to \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
Key points (move each point of the basic curve 1 unit left): \((-1,-\dfrac{\pi}{2})\to(-2,-\dfrac{\pi}{2})\); \((0,0)\to(-1,0)\); \((1,\dfrac{\pi}{2})\to(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2})\).

Compare: B has domain \([-2,0]\) and range \(\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) ✓. A is a shift RIGHT (\(\sin^{-1}(x-1)\), domain \([0,2]\)). C and D have the right domain \([-1,1]\) but ranges \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right]\) / \(\left[-\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]\), which would be a vertical shift \(\pm\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.note: x + 1 means shift LEFT 1: domain [−2, 0], range unchanged.

questions.stem: Evaluate the expression \(\tan\left(\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{5}\right)\right)\). Give your answer in the form of \(a\sqrt{b}\) where \(a\) and \(b\) are rational.
questions.hint: Let \(\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{5}\right)\), so \(\sin\alpha=-\dfrac{1}{5}\) with \(\alpha\) in \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) (4th quadrant: cosine POSITIVE). Draw a right triangle (opposite 1, hypotenuse 5), find the adjacent side by Pythagoras, then \(\tan\alpha=\dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}\) with the correct sign.

steps.explain: Give the angle a name. The range of \(\sin^{-1}\) is \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) and \(\sin\alpha<0\), so \(\alpha\) is in the 4th quadrant (below the \(x\)-axis).
Draw the reference right-angled triangle: opposite side \(1\) (red, pointing DOWN), hypotenuse \(5\) (blue). Find the adjacent side with Pythagoras.

steps.explain: Simplify the surd: \(\sqrt{24}=\sqrt{4\times6}=2\sqrt{6}\).
Tangent \(=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\). The opposite side is NEGATIVE (below the axis), the adjacent is positive (4th quadrant), so tangent is negative.
Rationalise the denominator: multiply top and bottom by \(\sqrt{6}\).
Write in the requested form \(a\sqrt{b}\) with \(a=-\dfrac{1}{12}\) and \(b=6\).

Check with a calculator: \(\sin^{-1}(-0.2)=-11.54^{\circ}\); \(\tan(-11.54^{\circ})=-0.2041\) ✓. Why not the others: B loses the negative sign; C uses \(\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{24}\) (a rationalising slip); D uses \(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt6}\to\dfrac{\sqrt6}{2}\).

questions.stem: Find the six solutions of the equation: \(\sin\left(2\cos^{-1}\left(\cot\left(2\tan^{-1}x\right)\right)\right)=0\). Give your answers as simplified surds
questions.hint: Work from the OUTSIDE in. \(\sin(\text{angle})=0\) means the angle is \(0,\pi\) (since \(2\cos^{-1}\) lies in \([0,2\pi]\)). So \(\cos^{-1}(\ldots)=0,\dfrac\pi2,\pi\), giving \(\cot(2\tan^{-1}x)=1,0,-1\). Then use \(\cot2\alpha=\dfrac{1-x^{2}}{2x}\) with \(x=\tan\alpha\).

steps.explain: Let \(\beta=\cos^{-1}(\cot(2\tan^{-1}x))\in[0,\pi]\). The equation is \(\sin2\beta=0\), so \(2\beta=0,\pi,2\pi\), i.e. \(\beta=0,\dfrac\pi2,\pi\). Then \(\cos\beta=1,\ 0,\ -1\).
Let \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}x\) (so \(x=\tan\alpha\)). Use \(\cot2\alpha=\dfrac{1}{\tan2\alpha}=\dfrac{1-\tan^{2}\alpha}{2\tan\alpha}=\dfrac{1-x^{2}}{2x}\).
Case \(=0\): \(1-x^{2}=0\Rightarrow x=\pm1\).
Case \(=1\): \(1-x^{2}=2x\Rightarrow x^{2}+2x-1=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt8}{2}=-1\pm\sqrt2\).
Case \(=-1\): \(1-x^{2}=-2x\Rightarrow x^{2}-2x-1=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt8}{2}=1\pm\sqrt2\).
Collect all six: \(\pm1\), and \(\sqrt2-1,\ -(\sqrt2-1)=1-\sqrt2,\ 1+\sqrt2,\ -(1+\sqrt2)\).

Check one: \(x=\sqrt2-1=\tan22.5^{\circ}\Rightarrow2\tan^{-1}x=45^{\circ}\Rightarrow\cot45^{\circ}=1\Rightarrow\cos^{-1}1=0\Rightarrow\sin0=0\) ✓. Why not the others: B (\(\pm\sqrt2,\ \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\)) solves \(2x^{2}\)-type equations; C includes \(0\) and \(\sqrt3\) (not solutions: \(\cot(0)\) is undefined); D is the cubic/\(\tan15^{\circ}\) set from a different problem.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Which of the following functions has a range of \([0,\pi]\)?
questions.hint: Know the basic ranges: \(\sin^{-1}\) gives \(\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]\); \(\cos^{-1}\) gives \([0,\pi]\). Absolute value \(|\ |\) makes negative outputs positive; a shift or stretch INSIDE changes the domain, not the range.

steps.explain: A: \(\sin^{-1}x\) has range \(\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]\). Taking the absolute value folds the negative part up: range \(\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]\). ✗
B: \(\cos^{-1}(x-1)\) is \(\cos^{-1}\) with a horizontal shift (domain \(0\le x\le2\)); the range is still \([0,\pi]\). It is already non-negative, so \(|\ |\) changes nothing. ✓
C: \(\sin^{-1}|x+1|\) has the input \(|x+1|\ge0\), so only the positive part of \(\sin^{-1}\) is used: range \(\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]\). ✗
D: \(\cos^{-1}|2x|\) has input \(|2x|\in[0,1]\), so \(\cos^{-1}\) takes only values from \(0\) to \(\dfrac\pi2\): range \(\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]\). ✗
Only B keeps the full range \([0,\pi]\).
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.note: \(\cos^{-1}\): \([0,\pi]\); \(|\cdot|\) inside shrinks it to \([0,\dfrac\pi2]\).

meta.source: Hills Grammar 2025 Trial HSC Mathematics Extension 1

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct
questions.hint: Test each statement with a number, e.g. \(x=\dfrac{1}{2}\) (or \(x=1\)). \(\sin^{-1}\) and \(\tan^{-1}\) are ODD functions (graph has half-turn symmetry); \(\cos^{-1}\) satisfies \(\cos^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cos^{-1}x\).

steps.explain: Test A with \(x=\dfrac{1}{2}\): \(\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=-\dfrac\pi6\) and \(-\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}=-\dfrac\pi6\). Equal ✓ (inverse sine is an ODD function).
Test B with \(x=0\): \(\cos^{-1}(0)=\dfrac\pi2\), but \(\pi+\cos^{-1}(0)=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), which is NOT even in the range \([0,\pi]\). ✗ (the true identity is \(\cos^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cos^{-1}x\)).
Test C with \(x=\dfrac{1}{2}\): \(\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=-\dfrac\pi6\ne\dfrac\pi6\). ✗
Test D with \(x=1\): \(\tan^{-1}(-1)=-\dfrac\pi4\ne\dfrac\pi4\). ✗ (\(\tan^{-1}\) is also odd: \(\tan^{-1}(-x)=-\tan^{-1}x\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Test with \(x=\dfrac{1}{2}\); \(\sin^{-1}\) is odd.

questions.stem: Which graph shows the curve \(y=\sin^{-1}(x+1)\)?
questions.hint: Start from \(y=\sin^{-1}x\) (domain \([-1,1]\), range \(\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]\), through the origin). Replacing \(x\) by \(x+1\) shifts the graph 1 unit LEFT (it does not change the range).

steps.explain: Basic graph \(y=\sin^{-1}x\): endpoints \(\left(-1,-\dfrac\pi2\right)\) and \(\left(1,\dfrac\pi2\right)\), passing through \((0,0)\).
\(y=\sin^{-1}(x+1)\): shift every point 1 unit to the LEFT (subtract 1 from each \(x\)).
Domain: \(-1\le x+1\le1\Rightarrow-2\le x\le0\). Range unchanged: \(-\dfrac\pi2\le y\le\dfrac\pi2\).
Why not the others: A is shifted RIGHT (\(\sin^{-1}(x-1)\)); C and D keep the domain \([-1,1]\) and have been shifted UP/DOWN by \(\dfrac\pi3\) (range \(-\dfrac\pi6\) to \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\)).
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.note: \(x\to x+1\): shift LEFT 1; domain \([-2,0]\).

questions.stem: Evaluate \(\sin^{-1}\left(\cos\left(\dfrac\pi6\right)\right)\)
questions.hint: Work from the INSIDE out: first find \(\cos\dfrac\pi6\) as an exact value, then ask “which angle in \(\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]\) has that sine?”

steps.explain: Exact value.
Now \(\sin^{-1}\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\): the angle in \(\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]\) whose sine is \(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) is \(60^{\circ}=\dfrac\pi3\).
Why not the others: B (\(\dfrac\pi6\)) wrongly cancels \(\sin^{-1}\) and \(\cos\) (\(\sin^{-1}\) only undoes \(\sin\)); C is outside the range \(\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]\); D has sine 1.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Inside first: \(\cos\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\).

questions.stem: Evaluate \(\cos\left(\tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)\) in exact value
questions.hint: Let \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\), so \(\tan\theta=-\dfrac{1}{3}\) with \(\theta\) in \(\left(-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right)\) (4th quadrant). Draw a right triangle with opposite 1 and adjacent 3, find the hypotenuse, then read \(\cos\theta\). In the 4th quadrant \(\cos\) is POSITIVE.

steps.explain: \(\tan\theta=-\dfrac{1}{3}\): ignore the sign for the triangle: opposite \(=1\), adjacent \(=3\).
The range of \(\tan^{-1}\) is \(\left(-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right)\): \(\theta\) is in the 4th quadrant (negative angle), where \(\cos\) is positive.
Rationalise if required: \(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}}=\dfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{10}\).
Why not the others: B is \(\sin\) (magnitude) not \(\cos\); C has the wrong sign (cos is positive in the 4th quadrant); D wrongly uses hypotenuse 4.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Triangle 1, 3, \(\sqrt{10}\); 4th quadrant: cos \(>0\).

questions.stem: Using the triangle below, or otherwise, simplify \(\sin^{-1}(\cos(x))\).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 240" width="100%" height="auto" style="max-width:330px;display:block;margin:0 auto"><polygon points="50,200 50,45 270,200" fill="#fff" fill-opacity="0.12" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="2.6"/><path d="M 50,182 L 68,182 L 68,200" fill="none" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 224,200 A 46 46 0 0 1 232.4,173.5" fill="none" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="2.6"/><text x="208.0" y="188.0" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3" paint-order="stroke" stroke-linejoin="round" font-style="italic">x</text><text x="40.0" y="122.5" text-anchor="end" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3" paint-order="stroke" stroke-linejoin="round" font-style="italic">1</text><text x="160.0" y="222.0" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3" paint-order="stroke" stroke-linejoin="round" font-style="italic">p</text></svg>

questions.hint: Use the complementary angle identity \(\cos x=\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)\). Then \(\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta)=\theta\) ONLY when \(\theta\) is in \(\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]\). In the triangle \(x\) is an acute angle, so \(\dfrac\pi2-x\) is also acute.

steps.explain: In the right-angled triangle the two acute angles add up to \(\dfrac\pi2\). The other acute angle is \(\dfrac\pi2-x\) (the angle at the top, see the diagram).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 240" width="100%" height="auto" style="max-width:330px;display:block;margin:0 auto"><polygon points="50,200 50,45 270,200" fill="#7c3aed" fill-opacity="0.12" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="2.6"/><path d="M 50,182 L 68,182 L 68,200" fill="none" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 224,200 A 46 46 0 0 1 232.4,173.5" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.6"/><text x="208.0" y="188.0" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="800" fill="#dc2626" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3" paint-order="stroke" stroke-linejoin="round" font-style="italic">x</text><text x="40.0" y="122.5" text-anchor="end" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="800" fill="#3b4ea8" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3" paint-order="stroke" stroke-linejoin="round" font-style="italic">1</text><text x="160.0" y="222.0" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="800" fill="#3b4ea8" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3" paint-order="stroke" stroke-linejoin="round" font-style="italic">p</text><text x="172.0" y="114.5" text-anchor="start" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="800" fill="#047857" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3" paint-order="stroke" stroke-linejoin="round">hyp</text></svg>

steps.explain: Compare the sides: \(\cos x=\dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}=\dfrac{p}{\text{hyp}}\). For the TOP angle \(\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)\), the side opposite it is the side \(p\). So the sine of the top angle is the same ratio.
Substitute and use the range: \(\dfrac\pi2-x\) lies in \(\left(0,\dfrac\pi2\right)\subset\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]\), so \(\sin^{-1}\) just returns the angle.
Why not the others: B (\(x\)) wrongly cancels \(\sin^{-1}\) with \(\cos\); C and D give angles outside the range of \(\sin^{-1}\) or with the wrong sign.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: What is the value of \(\cos^{-1}(\tan x)+\sin^{-1}(\tan x)\) for \(-\dfrac\pi4\le x\le\dfrac\pi4\) ?
questions.hint: For any \(u\) in \([-1,1]\): \(\sin^{-1}u+\cos^{-1}u=\dfrac\pi2\). Check that \(\tan x\) really lies in \([-1,1]\) for the given \(x\).

steps.explain: For \(-\dfrac\pi4\le x\le\dfrac\pi4\), \(\tan x\) goes from \(-1\) to \(1\): so \(u=\tan x\) is in the domain \([-1,1]\) of both \(\sin^{-1}\) and \(\cos^{-1}\).
Complementary identity: \(\sin^{-1}u+\cos^{-1}u=\dfrac\pi2\) (e.g. \(u=0\): \(0+\dfrac\pi2\); \(u=1\): \(\dfrac\pi2+0\)).
Why not the others: B (0) and C (1) are numbers it never equals; D (\(\pi\)) is double the true value.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\sin^{-1}u+\cos^{-1}u=\dfrac\pi2\)

questions.stem: Sketch the graph of the function \(f(x)=-2\tan^{-1}x\) showing the intercepts on the axes and the equations of the asymptotes. Which sketch (A–D) is correct?
questions.hint: Start with \(y=\tan^{-1}x\): increasing, through the origin, horizontal asymptotes \(y=\pm\dfrac\pi2\). The factor 2 STRETCHES vertically (asymptotes become \(\pm\pi\)) and the MINUS reflects it in the \(x\)-axis (so the curve is DECREASING).

steps.explain: Basic graph \(y=\tan^{-1}x\): passes through \((0,0)\), asymptotes \(y=\dfrac\pi2\) (right) and \(y=-\dfrac\pi2\) (left).
Multiply by 2 (vertical stretch): asymptotes \(y=\pm2\times\dfrac\pi2=\pm\pi\). The origin stays where it is.
Multiply by \(-1\) (reflect in the \(x\)-axis): the curve now FALLS from \(y=\pi\) on the left to \(y=-\pi\) on the right.

Intercepts: \(x=0\Rightarrow y=0\); \(y=0\Rightarrow x=0\): only the origin. Why not the others: B is \(+2\tan^{-1}x\) (increasing); C is \(-\tan^{-1}x\) (asymptotes \(\pm\dfrac\pi2\)); D is \(-\tan^{-1}2x\) (also \(\pm\dfrac\pi2\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: showing the intercepts on the axes and the equations of the asymptotes.
keyPoints.note: Reflect and stretch \(\tan^{-1}x\): asymptotes \(y=\pm\pi\).
